messages.subject: DSM questions
parts:
Dear Distance Samplers,

I have a couple of basic questions relating to DSM. My my data are transect samples for ungulates in a Kenyan nature conservancy. I have been going through this very helpful vignette -> http://distancesampling.org/R/vignettes/mexico-analysis.html and seem to have some initial results for population density. 

My questions are:

1 - Is it possible to overlay a basic response plot (see attached) that was generated using vis.gam with a map that was generated using ggmap? I used:
    
    naboishoMap <- qmap('Naboisho', maptype="satellite", zoom=14)

, to grab the map image. I dont think it's rasta from what I can tell?

2 - I used a tweedie distribution to generate my dsm - and I get the following (Attached) when I run gam.check. The Q-Q plot doesn't look too hot, and I'm not 100% sure how to interpret the remaining plots. I'd be very grateful for any advice on how to interpret them, and also if there is a better distribution I should use?

Thank you

Anthony

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM questions
parts:
Hi Anthony, hi listfolk,

Quick reply to these:

1. it's not possible to get vis.gam to talk to ggmap as they use
different plotting systems. Instead you need to make predictions over
some grid of the space/other covariates then plot that using ggplot's
geom_tile, you can then add in a ggmap. Two important things here: 1.
(perhaps obviously) you need to turn down the opacity on the geom_tile
layer to see the background, 2. the prediction grid needs to have all
your covariates in it, note that vis.gam will take averages for the
covariates not displayed (median for continuous, mode for factors), so
the plot you currently have may not be accurate depending on your model
(see the cond argument to vis.gam for more information).

2. Regarding the plots, the Q-Q plot doesn't look great, you're right.
You could try using the negative binomial distribution (nb() in mgcv).
Resids. vs linear predictor plot is not interpretable in this form as
for count data it's hard to see any patterns in the deviance residuals,
use rqgam.check to get a better version using randomised quantile
residuals (and see the reference therein for how to interpret). A full
explanation of the gam.check output is available in Simon Wood's GAM book.

cheers,
--dave

I'm struggling to unpack the dsm data object and apply it successfully in ggplot using geom_tile. So previously I can visualise the smooth with:

All good. So to get the same plot using ggplot, I need to take dsm.xy and do something like:

preddata$density <- predict(dsm.xy, newdata=preddata)

p <- ggplot(predgrid) +
      geom_tile(aes(x=x, y=y)

print(p)

However, I just get a complete mess!

Thanks

Anthony

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM questions
parts:
No worries Anthony.

ggplot-wise you're almost there, you're missing the fill= aesthetic to
ensure that the tiles have colours. You'll need something like:


p <- ggplot(predgrid) +
geom_tile(aes(x=x, y=y, fill=density)

note that depending on the exact setup of your prediction grid you may
need other aesthetics (e.g., width and height).

I can recommend stackoverflow or the resources at
https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/ for more ggplot2 advice.


cheers,
--dave
